title: Core Web Vitals in plain language
excerpt: Core Web Vitals explained: how fast the main content appears, how fast a tap responds, and whether the page jumps. The good thresholds are 2.5s, 200ms, and 0.1.
alt: A long, quiet office corridor with glass rooms, a teal sofa, and a dark kitchen. The still corridor fits a piece about whether a page stays stable and readable.
caption: Three questions: did it appear, did it respond, did it jump. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What are Core Web Vitals?
faqs.answer: They are three measures of page experience. Largest Contentful Paint is when the main content appears, Interaction to Next Paint is how long a tap waits before the next frame, and Cumulative Layout Shift is how much the page jumps. web.dev publishes the good thresholds: within 2.5 seconds, 200 milliseconds or less, and 0.1 or less.

faqs.question: Do good scores guarantee search rankings?
faqs.answer: No. They describe whether the page is pleasant to use, and Google's search documentation treats page experience as one part of what ranking systems reward, not as a prize for hitting a number. A fast page with nothing to say will not outrank a clear one. A clear page that jumps and stalls still wastes the visit.

faqs.question: Which number should a founder look at?
faqs.answer: The 75th percentile, not the best load. web.dev recommends judging the metrics at the 75th percentile of page loads, split by mobile and desktop. A single demo on the office network can look perfect while a quarter of visitors get something worse. Ask for the field number, from real visits, once the site has traffic.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
Core Web Vitals explained for a founder are three questions about a page. Did the main thing appear quickly? Did the page respond when someone tapped? Did the layout stay still while they tried to read or click? The names are Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint, and Cumulative Layout Shift. You can run the company without the names. You should not ship a marketing site without the questions.

[web.dev](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) publishes the thresholds for a good experience. Largest Contentful Paint should happen within 2.5 seconds of the page starting to load. Interaction to Next Paint should be 200 milliseconds or less. Cumulative Layout Shift should be 0.1 or less. A page is in good shape on these measures when it meets those targets at the 75th percentile of loads, looked at separately for mobile and desktop. The best load on a new laptop is not the number.

## Largest Contentful Paint

Largest Contentful Paint is the moment the largest visible piece of content appears. On a company homepage that is usually the hero image or the main headline, whichever occupies more of the first screen. Until that moment, the page has not really arrived, even if a background or a menu already has.

Picture a founder sending the homepage to a buyer. The buyer opens it on a phone between meetings. The largest thing should be the sentence that says what the company does, or the picture that shows the product. If that sentence waits on a font, or the picture is several times bigger than the slot it sits in, the paint is late. The buyer sees a header and a wait. Two and a half seconds is the line web.dev draws for a good score. Past it, the wait is the experience.

What usually causes the miss is ordinary. An uncompressed photograph. A video used as a background. A custom font that blocks the text. A script that has to run before anything is allowed to show. None of these are mysterious. They are choices that put a file in front of the sentence.

## Interaction to Next Paint

Interaction to Next Paint measures the wait between an input and the next frame the person can see. A tap on the menu, a click on Book a call, a keystroke in a form. The clock runs until the screen shows a response. web.dev's good line is 200 milliseconds or less.

Picture the same buyer tapping the only button that matters. The button should change, or the next view should start, almost immediately. If the page is busy running an animation library, a chat widget, and three analytics tags, the tap sits in a queue. The site feels broken even when it is only slow. People repeat the tap. The second tap fires late, on the wrong thing, and now you have a real bug made out of lag.

An older measure, First Input Delay, used to stand in for this idea. web.dev notes that Interaction to Next Paint replaced it as the stable Core Web Vital in 2024, because a single first input did not describe the whole visit. If a report still talks about the old name, ask for the newer one. You want the wait on interactions, not a legacy score.

## Cumulative Layout Shift

Cumulative Layout Shift measures visual stability. Content that moves after it has started to appear, without the person asking it to, adds to the score. web.dev's good line is 0.1 or less. A zero would mean nothing jumped. A large number means the page rearranged itself under the reader's eyes.

Picture a button near the bottom of a short screen. The buyer goes to tap it. A late banner, an image without a reserved height, or a font that swaps and changes the line breaks pushes the button down. The tap hits something else, or hits nothing. The buyer feels foolish. The site caused it.

Reserve space for images. Do not inject a bar above the headline after load. Be careful with embeds. Movement that follows a tap, because the person opened a menu, is not the same kind of surprise. The metric is about movement they did not ask for.

## How this relates to search, and how it does not

Google Search Central documents [Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) as part of how page experience is discussed in search. Use that page when you want the search product's own wording. Use web.dev when you want the definitions and the thresholds. Neither page is a promise that a perfect score will rank a thin site. A homepage that says nothing clear will not be rescued by a fast paint. A homepage that says something clear, and then jumps while people try to use it, wastes the visit it managed to earn.

Treat the numbers as a quality bar for the build, the way you treat a sentence a stranger can understand. Hanabi holds the marketing site to that bar because the page is the product we are willing to show. The practical habit is to look at a phone, then look at the field data once real visits exist. Lab tools can catch a regression before launch. Field data tells you what visitors got. web.dev is explicit that the lab is not a substitute for the field, because devices, networks, and behavior differ.

## What to ask a studio

Ask for the three numbers on the templates that matter: the homepage, a content page, and the page with the form. Ask for them on mobile. Ask what the largest element is, and whether it is the element you care about. Ask what can shift after load. Ask for the still version of any motion, so a score is not bought by removing the page's only explanation.

You can watch for the failures without a dashboard. If you can read the offer immediately, tap the action without a stall, and trust the page not to jump, the vitals are probably in a decent place. If you cannot, a dashboard will only confirm the annoyance you already felt.

Speed is the reason to care, and cleverness is what usually spends it. [Why a marketing site should be fast before it is clever](/blog/fast-before-clever) is the companion piece, about putting the readable page ahead of the animation.

When you want a site held to those thresholds as part of the build, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The plain version of the standard is that the page appears, responds, and stays still.
